title: Objects, abstraction and responsibility boundaries
goal: Build a domain model and explain why its operations preserve an invariant.

prerequisites.text: Modules 1–4: input, functions, sequences, ownership, testing and multifile builds.

sections.title: From a record to a domain object
paragraphs: In Module 3 a structure grouped related data, such as a sensor reading and its unit. In the language an object has storage, a type and a lifetime; an int variable is an object too. Design uses a more specific idea: a representation of a domain concept together with the operations allowed on it.

Not every record needs a hierarchy. If every combination of fields is meaningful, a plain struct with public data and free functions can be clearer. When values must satisfy a relationship, such as a counter remaining between zero and one hundred, the type should control changes. Begin with that requirement rather than with class syntax.

sections.title: Reading a first class
paragraphs: In Counter the name after class declares a new type. The value_ field belongs separately to each instance, and =0 supplies its initial value. Members before public: are private in a class. Members after public: form operations callers can use. The semicolon following the closing brace completes the class declaration.

Counter a,b creates two independent objects. Calling a.add(7) selects a, so value_ inside the method denotes a's field. The value() const method observes state; const prevents ordinary modification of fields through this object. Constructors receive their own lesson. For now, a field initializer and the automatically generated constructor establish the starting state.

sections.title: Worked model
paragraphs: Build a domain model and explain why its operations preserve an invariant.
steps: Create records with an accepted and a rejected value.
Compare bool results one and zero.

sections.title: Invariant and operation contract
paragraphs: An invariant is a statement that holds after construction and after every public operation finishes. Counter promises a value between zero and one hundred. The add contract accepts only a nonnegative increment that fits the remaining capacity. Success returns true; rejection returns false and preserves the previous value. These are observable promises that tests can check.

The n>100-value_ check happens before addition. Testing value_+n>100 is less safe because a sufficiently large n could overflow int before comparison. Here the remaining capacity stays within zero to one hundred, and the first condition rejects negative increments. The pre-call invariant and these checks justify the post-call invariant, beyond a single successful demonstration.

sections.title: Abstraction hides decisions
paragraphs: A caller needs add and value, rather than the spelling or representation of a private field. The representation can later change while the contract remains stable. Abstraction selects the observable properties needed for a task. This reduces the number of details a reader must hold in mind when checking a program.

Hiding a field alone does not create a useful interface. Unrestricted getValue/setValue operations can still violate the meaning of a type. Names such as reserve, ship or accept express intent and conditions better than a universal setter. Conversely, a simple immutable record should not acquire methods merely to look object oriented.

sections.title: Responsibility and dependencies
paragraphs: The counter is responsible for a valid value, not for reading cin, selecting a UI language or saving a project. Separation lets you test an object without a browser or a file. The application parses input first, invokes domain operations second and formats output last. Each part has a distinct reason to change.

Do not move every function into a giant Application class. Examine responsibilities by asking which requirement would force this code to change. A new input format should not require changing counter arithmetic. Collaboration between small types is often more useful than a deep hierarchy; inheritance comes after ownership and contracts in this module.

sections.title: Contract boundary check
paragraphs: Build a domain model and explain why its operations preserve an invariant.
steps: Each Counter starts with its own zero.
Seven succeeds; ninety-four is rejected before mutation.

sections.title: Testing two objects
paragraphs: In the worked example a accepts seven, then rejects ninety-four, while b remains zero. The output is 7 0 0: the first state, the second state and the last success flag. That final zero does not indicate a damaged object. Rejection is an expected operation result, distinct from a malformed input stream.

An independent test should modify only a and observe b. It catches an accidentally shared static field. Also test repeated rejection, a zero increment and filling exactly to capacity. Compare state before and after a rejected call. Checking only the returned bool misses an implementation that changes a field before returning false.

sections.title: Laboratory protocol
paragraphs: The laboratory reads an operation count from zero to twenty and exactly that many integer increments. It validates all input syntax before producing a domain result. An increment such as minus one or one hundred and one is a domain rejection and increases rejected. An unknown token or a missing number makes the entire input invalid.

For three increments 30 80 20, the state trace is zero, thirty, thirty, fifty, with one rejection. Write that trace before running the program. Test the maximum int separately: the contract rejects it without overflowing. The supplied cases are checkable examples; add an independent case and an invariant explanation rather than relying solely on matching stdout.

sections.title: Choosing a model
paragraphs: Compare two solutions to the same task: an open structure with a validation function, and a class with private state. Identify places where the first permits a forgotten check and describe the extra code required by the second. Choose object oriented design for manageable dependencies and invariants, rather than assuming every free function needs a class.

During review explain who owns state, who can change it and what a test observes. These runs do not establish safety for arbitrary programs. They support a contract for a bounded model and specific checked cases. The next lesson develops interfaces with related fields, const correctness and operations that preserve several conditions together.

selfcheck.prompt: What happens when add(101) is called on zero?
selfcheck.feedback: The capacity check runs before assigning the field, so 101 cannot fit in the remaining 100. Returning false reports rejection; it neither stores the rejected value nor requires an exception.

options: It is always faster than subtraction.
To check capacity before a potentially unsafe addition.
selfcheck.feedback: The expression value_+n could overflow before comparison. Subtraction is safe because the invariant bounds value_ to 0…100, while the earlier n<0 check rejects negative increments.

selfcheck.prompt: Does every record need a class?
options: Only if the record stores int.
No; the choice depends on invariants and responsibility.
selfcheck.feedback: A class is justified when its operations must jointly protect a constraint or responsibility. For a plain record whose states are all valid, a public struct and free functions may be clearer.

selfcheck.prompt: What does an independent second instance check?
options: The absence of accidentally shared state.
selfcheck.feedback: Changing only a should leave b unchanged, exposing an accidental static field in place of instance state. This tests independence, not performance or include order.

selfcheck.prompt: What does private provide by itself?
options: A compile-time restriction on ordinary access.
selfcheck.feedback: private restricts ordinary client access to a member at compile time. It does not encrypt bytes or validate ranges; the public operations must implement those checks.

practice.title: Laboratory: Objects, abstraction and responsibility boundaries
practice.task: Read n=0…20 and exactly n integer increments. Counter starts at zero and accepts a nonnegative increment only if it fits the remaining capacity of 100; rejection preserves state. Print the value and rejection count separated by a space. Invalid syntax, count or trailing tokens: invalid.
criteria: Identify the value, add, value() and initial zero.
Explain remaining-capacity bounds and the risk of value+n.
Changing one leaves the other unchanged.
Include source, actual results, an independent case and limits of the conclusion.

The add contract accepts only a nonnegative increment that fits the remaining capacity. Success returns true; rejection returns false and preserves the previous value. These are observable promises that tests can check.

steps.action: Restate the contract and distinguish malformed input from domain rejection.

Complete the starter; pending marks unfinished work rather than a correct result.
Run every reference case and record actual stdout and exit status.

terms.definition: Storage with a type and lifetime; it need not be an instance of a user-defined class.
Selected observable properties that hide decisions a client does not need.
A condition established at construction and preserved by public operations.
Conditions governing valid calls, results, effects and rejection.
Values that determine an object's subsequent observable behaviour.
A function member invoked on a selected object.
A coherent task assigned to a type and a reason for changing its code.
A particular object of a type with its own state.
